extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general educated public interested in manners, theatre, charity, and marriage
extracted.subtask_description: Short 18th-century moral/satirical essays discussing social behaviour, theatre etiquette, charity policy, and conjugal conduct intended for a general literate readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shame-faced false modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Decency of Behaviour, all outward Show of Virtue, and Abhorrence of Vice, are carefully avoided by this set of shame-faced people, as what would disparage their Gayety of Temper, and infallibly bring them to Dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer condemns a modesty that is mere affectation: such behaviour is described as 'Poorness of Spirit' and 'despicable Cowardice.' It is presented as a moral failing evident in ordinary conversation and to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face involuntary defects with noble spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another kind of vicious Modesty which makes a Man ashamed of his Person, his Birth, his Profession, his Poverty, or the like Misfortunes, which it was not in his Choice to prevent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than being out of countenance, a person should 'exert a noble Spirit' and palliate imperfections by those perfections which are in his power; literary allusion: 'imitate Cæsar, who, because his Head was bald, cover'd that Defect with Laurels.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict indiscriminate alms to avoid promoting idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: No Man should be permitted to take Relief from the Parish, or to ask it in the Street, till he has first purchased as much as possible of his own Livelihood by the Labour of his own Hands; and then the Publick ought only to be taxed to make good the Deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument (Sir Andrew) that liberality to common beggars supplies wages of idleness, reduces available labour, and raises prices; increasing the number of working hands would reduce manufacturing costs and expand markets, benefiting national interests. Practical consequence: favour measures that encourage labour before relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise charity toward the industrious and truly afflicted
rubrics_metrics.description: I know of no Virtue in the Gospel that is in more pathetical Expressions recommended to our Practice... I shall endeavour to obey the Will of my Lord and Master: And therefore if an industrious Man shall submit to the hardest Labour and coarsest Fare, rather than endure the Shame of taking Relief... this is the Hungry, the Thirsty, the Naked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charity is endorsed for those who are industrious or in genuine need (strangers, captives, prisoners, invalid hospitals), but not for 'an Alms-house of idle People' who will not reform; the ministerially deserving should receive support aimed at restoring useful subjects, not sustaining profligacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolent falsehoods can be excused when they do good
rubrics_metrics.description: The officious Liar many have argued is to be excused, because it does some Man good, and no Man hurt. The Man who made more than ordinary speed from a Fight... told them they had obtained a complete Victory, and put the whole City into the utmost Joy and Exultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lying to keep up spirits (physician to patient), inventing praise to reconcile quarrels or to raise cheerfulness. The essay treats such 'lies' as socially useful when they produce happiness and no harm, and when they are used to coax reconciliation and good humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest additions to a story are amiable when harmless
rubrics_metrics.description: You very often hear People, after a Story has been told with some entertaining Circumstances, tell it over again with Particulars that destroy the Jest, but give Light into the Truth of the Narration. This sort of Veracity, though it is impertinent, has something amiable in it, because it proceeds from the Love of Truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retelling with truthful particulars that spoil a jest is impertinent but acceptable out of love of truth; such amendments make someone a 'sincere Friend' rather than merely an entertaining companion—worth allowing modest time to correct harmless matters of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-thinking requires reasoned coherence, not licentiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: They who value themselves upon that conceited Title were a little better instructed in what it ought to stand for; and that they would not persuade themselves a Man is really and truly a Free-thinker in any tolerable Sense, meerly by virtue of his being an Atheist, or an Infidel of any other Distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of contemporary 'free-thinkers' as being licentious rather than disciplined: they disdain Deduction, Coherence, Consistency, and the Rules of Reason as 'too precise and mechanical.' True free-thinking should be governed by reason, not mere wantonness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical applause benefits from a skilled leader (the 'Trunk-maker')
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a certain Person in the upper Gallery of the Playhouse... who when he is pleased with any Thing that is acted upon the Stage, expresses his Approbation by a loud Knock upon the Benches or the Wainscot... He has saved many a good Play, and brought many a graceful Actor into Reputation, who would not otherwise have been taken notice of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single well-timed, vigorous signal can awaken audience attention and generate applause that helps actors' reputations. The essay humorously proposes formalising the role, paid for life, to ensure consistent direction of public taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for a public-applause director
rubrics_metrics.description: To the End that this Place should be always disposed of according to Merit, I would have none preferred to it, who has not given convincing Proofs both of a sound Judgment and a strong Arm...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed (tongue-in-cheek) job requirements: proven sound judgment and physical force (able to 'knock down an Ox, or write a Comment upon Horace's Art of Poetry'); a combination of Herculean strength and artistic discernment (composition of Hercules and Apollo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applause must be well-timed and can be decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been observed, his Blow is so well timed, that the most judicious Critick could never except against it... If the Audience does not concur with him, he smites a second Time, and if the Audience is not yet awaked, looks round him with great Wrath, and repeats the Blow a third Time, which never fails to produce the Clap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper timing of approval cues is essential: a decisive, well-placed signal can trigger collective response; actors value applause more when it is convincingly led, and spurious or weak applause is 'Brutum fulmen'—empty noise—without authoritative accompaniment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid returning evil for good in marriage; practice civility
rubrics_metrics.description: Is any Thing more unlike a Gentleman, than when his Honour is engaged for the performing his Promises... to become afterwards false to his Word, and be alone the Occasion of Misery to one whose Happiness he but lately pretended was dearer to him than his own?... A kind Look they believe would be fawning, and a civil Answer yielding the Superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against husbands treating wives with contempt or affected moroseness to appear 'free' or 'masterly.' Recommends persuading men that voluntary civility, tenderness, and good breeding toward a wife are signs of greatness of soul, will make marriage more pleasant, and avoid alienating affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn detraction into reconciliation via strategic flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst Evil I ever observed this Man's Falsehood occasion, has been that he turned Detraction into Flattery. He is well skilled in the Manners of the World, and by over-looking what Men really are, he grounds his Artifices upon what they have a Mind to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: exaggerate or invent appearances that flatter both parties to resolve quarrels; by making each think the other admired, the officious mediator creates mutual amends and renewed convivial relations—presented as socially useful, though morally ambiguous.
